unit.why: A brief anecdote, quoted from an earlier book, about the pre-Hasidic author of Avodat ha-Gershuni, who paid a scholar to watch him and rebuke him at once; it is a habitual practice rather than a single event, so it is a borderline story.
unit.boundary_note: part of a chain of cited exempla on accepting rebuke; the next division starts a parallel anecdote about the Maharshal

stories.start_quote: ובס׳ זת״מ בהק׳ וז״ל ומי לנו
stories.end_quote: יאמר לו תיכף שעשה שלא כהוגן
stories.summary_en: The gaon, author of Avodat ha-Gershuni, kept a Torah scholar on salary to stay with him always, watch all his deeds, words and movements, and tell him at once whenever he acted improperly.

tags.why: praises a pre-Hasidic rabbinic authority; the anecdote is copied from an earlier book
cited as an exemplum in a chain teaching about seeking rebuke

quotes: ומה שלא תישר בעיניו יאמר לו תיכף שעשה שלא כהוגן
tags.why: a great sage submits himself to correction by another
the point of the anecdote is moral self-scrutiny
illustrates a sage's virtue, though the sage is not a tsaddik in the Hasidic sense

missing_concepts: seeking rebuke / tokhehah (hiring a personal admonisher)
